doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

chapter: Learning and views on jazz history
title: Why bebop had a smaller popular audience
summary: Ingham thinks bebop was urban small-group music with no whistleable tunes, contrasted with songs like 'Blues in the Night'.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: I think it had a small audience — well I say small — I mean it certainly took off in a way I think, when you look back on it, but it was the urban areas. I mean first of all there were some big bands of course, like Billy Eckstine’s band and Dizzy Gillespie took a big band out. But they were playing charts, and sometimes people didn’t hear that thing they could dance to quite so much. But bebop essentially I think was small group things and it was musicians perhaps playing, I’m not saying for themselves, but it was very innovative of course, and I think it was the urban centers like New York maybe and L.A. certainly, those two sort of extremes, and then I think, I wouldn’t say it had a big, big audience but certainly there were people playing it all around Detroit and those urban areas where there were jazz clubs and where people heard it. And Charlie Parker would go to those clubs as a guest artist. I think he probably did reach a big audience, I’m sure he did, but I don’t think that, there wasn’t that kind of commercial possibility to pick up on it. And secondly, most of the things were songs, they didn’t have lyrics to them, how are you going to remember a line like “Donna Lee” — it’s “Indiana” basically, the song, but you can’t sing [scats]. I mean it’s the same chord structure but it’s the same thing “What Is This Thing Called Love” is that “Hothouse” [scats]. No.
Which one is easier to whistle?

“What Is This Thing Called Love,” exactly. That’s a good point because something that was commercially possible, people could whistle it, you know, the humblest guy. And it’s a very interesting point you say that, because one of the hardest songs probably written is “Blues In The Night.” There’s a middle strain on it, eight bar, it’s a kind of complicated [scats]. Harold Arlen and Johnny Mercer. That was probably one of their biggest hits simply because that catchy opening phrase: “My mommy done told me” [scats/whistles]. You know, going around, here comes the paper boy [whistles]. That’s it.
